units.title: Kinematics with Calculus
units.blurb: Velocity and acceleration as derivatives, motion found by integrating, and motion in two and three dimensions.

units.title: Forces with Calculus
units.blurb: Time-varying forces, drag, banked curves, pulley constraints and the center of mass by integration.

units.title: Work and Energy with Calculus
units.blurb: Work as an integral, potential energy from force and force from potential energy, and energy diagrams.

units.title: Momentum and Systems of Particles
units.blurb: Impulse as an integral, collisions in two dimensions, systems of particles and rockets.

units.title: Rotation of Rigid Bodies
units.blurb: Moments of inertia by integration, torque and angular momentum as cross products, rolling, rotational collisions and equilibrium.

units.title: Gravitation and Orbits
units.blurb: Gravity of spheres, orbital energy, Kepler's laws from Newton's, and elliptical orbits.

units.title: Oscillations with Calculus
units.blurb: Simple harmonic motion as a differential equation, physical pendulums, damping and resonance.

topics.title: Velocity as a Derivative
topics.short: v = dx/dt gives the velocity at any instant from the position function.
topics.trouble: Students divide x(t) by t, finding an average velocity from the origin instead of the derivative.

topics.title: Acceleration as a Derivative
topics.short: a = dv/dt = d²x/dt², and zero velocity at an instant says nothing about the acceleration.
topics.trouble: Students think an object with zero velocity at an instant must have zero acceleration there.

topics.title: Velocity and Position from Acceleration
topics.short: Integrate a(t) once for v(t) and again for x(t), using the starting values to fix the constants.
topics.trouble: Students forget the constants of integration, losing the starting velocity or position.

topics.title: Deriving the Constant-Acceleration Equations
topics.short: Integrating a constant acceleration twice gives the familiar equations and shows exactly when they apply.
topics.trouble: Students use constant-acceleration equations for an acceleration that changes with time.

topics.title: Acceleration That Depends on Position
topics.short: When a depends on x, write a = v dv/dx and integrate over x.
topics.trouble: Students integrate a(x) with respect to t, as if it were a function of time.

topics.title: Position, Velocity and Acceleration Vectors
topics.short: r(t), v = dr/dt and a = dv/dt describe motion in two and three dimensions, one component at a time.
topics.trouble: Students think the acceleration vector always points along the velocity, even on a curved path.

topics.title: Projectiles with Calculus
topics.short: Use derivatives to find the highest point, the range and the launch angle that goes farthest.
topics.trouble: Students set the whole velocity, not just its vertical part, to zero at the top of the path.

topics.title: Relative Motion and Galilean Frames
topics.short: Frames moving at constant velocity disagree about velocities but agree about accelerations and forces.
topics.trouble: Students think the acceleration also changes between frames that move at constant velocity.

topics.title: Tangential and Centripetal Acceleration
topics.short: On a curve, acceleration splits into dv/dt along the path and v²/r toward the center.
topics.trouble: Students take the whole acceleration to be v²/r even while the speed is changing.

topics.title: Motion Under a Time-Varying Force
topics.short: Integrate F(t)/m to find the velocity when the force changes with time.
topics.trouble: Students use the final force as if it had acted the whole time.

topics.title: Linear Drag and Terminal Velocity
topics.short: With drag F = −bv, the speed approaches v_T = mg/b as v(t) = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)), with τ = m/b.
topics.trouble: Students think a falling object stops speeding up because gravity weakens, or that it reaches terminal speed after a finite time.

topics.title: Quadratic Drag
topics.short: Fast objects in air feel drag ½CρAv², which gives a terminal speed √(2mg/(CρA)).
topics.trouble: Students think heavier objects would fall faster even in a vacuum, because they do in air.

topics.title: Banked Curves With and Without Friction
topics.short: Find the design speed of a banked road and the range of speeds friction allows.
topics.trouble: Students split the normal force along the slope as on a ramp, instead of horizontally and vertically.

topics.title: Constraints in Pulley Systems
topics.short: The fixed length of a rope links the accelerations, so a movable pulley gives a₁ = 2a₂.
topics.trouble: Students give both masses the same acceleration when a movable pulley halves one of them.

topics.title: Center of Mass by Integration
topics.short: x_cm = (1/M)∫x dm, with dm = λ dx for a rod whose density varies.
topics.trouble: Students forget to divide by the total mass, or integrate x without the density.

topics.title: Work by a Variable Force
topics.short: W = ∫F dx, the area under the force–position curve.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the force by the distance when the force changes along the way.

topics.title: Work Along a Path
topics.short: W = ∫F · dr adds up only the part of the force along each small step of the path.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the size of the force by the path length, ignoring the angle between them.

topics.title: The Work-Energy Theorem from Newton's Second Law
topics.short: Integrating m dv/dt over x turns F = ma into W_net = ΔK.
topics.trouble: Students use the work of one force, not the net work, to find the change in kinetic energy.

topics.title: Conservative Forces
topics.short: A force is conservative when its work doesn't depend on the path, so its work around any closed loop is zero.
topics.trouble: Students think friction does the same work on any path between two points.

topics.title: Potential Energy from Force
topics.short: U(x) = −∫F dx, which gives ½kx² for a spring and mgy for uniform gravity.
topics.trouble: Students drop the minus sign, so the potential energy falls where it should rise.

topics.title: Force from Potential Energy
topics.short: F = −dU/dx: the force points downhill on the potential energy curve.
topics.trouble: Students think the force points toward higher potential energy.

topics.title: Potential Energy Diagrams
topics.short: Read turning points, allowed regions and stable or unstable equilibria from a graph of U(x).
topics.trouble: Students think an object can pass through a region where its total energy is less than U.

topics.title: Instantaneous Power
topics.short: P = dW/dt = F · v gives the power at each instant.
topics.trouble: Students use the average power when the force or speed is changing.

topics.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Escape Speed
topics.short: From U = −GMm/r, the escape speed is √(2GM/r), the same for any mass.
topics.trouble: Students think a heavier object needs a higher escape speed.

topics.title: Impulse as an Integral
topics.short: J = ∫F dt for any force that changes in time.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the peak force by the collision time.

topics.title: Solving Elastic Collisions
topics.short: Combine conservation of momentum and of kinetic energy: the relative speed reverses in a one-dimensional elastic collision.
topics.trouble: Students write only the momentum equation and are left with one equation for two unknowns.

topics.title: Collisions in Two Dimensions
topics.short: Conserve the x- and y-components of momentum separately.
topics.trouble: Students conserve the total speed instead of each component of momentum.

topics.title: Newton's Second Law for a System
topics.short: ΣF_external = M·a_cm, because the internal forces cancel in pairs.
topics.trouble: Students include forces between parts of the system when finding the acceleration of the center of mass.

topics.title: The Rocket Equation
topics.short: A rocket gains Δv = v_e ln(m₀/m_f) by throwing mass backward.
topics.trouble: Students think a rocket moves by pushing against the air or the ground.

topics.title: Angular Velocity and Acceleration with Calculus
topics.short: ω = dθ/dt and α = dω/dt; integrate α(t) to find ω and θ.
topics.trouble: Students differentiate an angle given in degrees and treat the result as radians per second.

topics.title: Moment of Inertia by Integration
topics.short: I = ∫r² dm gives the rotational inertia of rods, rings, disks and spheres.
topics.trouble: Students use the distance to the center of mass instead of the distance to the axis.

topics.title: The Parallel-Axis Theorem
topics.short: I = I_cm + Md² for an axis shifted a distance d from the center of mass.
topics.trouble: Students apply the theorem starting from an axis that doesn't pass through the center of mass.

topics.title: Torque as a Cross Product
topics.short: τ = r × F, with its direction given by the right-hand rule.
topics.trouble: Students measure r from the wrong point, or reverse the order to F × r.

topics.title: Rolling Dynamics
topics.short: Static friction makes rolling work: on a ramp a = g sin θ/(1 + I/(MR²)).
topics.trouble: Students think static friction takes energy from an object rolling without slipping.

topics.title: From Skidding to Rolling
topics.short: A ball that starts out sliding skids until v = Rω, losing energy to kinetic friction on the way.
topics.trouble: Students assume a thrown bowling ball rolls without slipping from the moment it lands.

topics.title: Angular Momentum of a Particle
topics.short: L = r × p, so even a particle moving in a straight line has angular momentum about a point.
topics.trouble: Students think a particle needs to move in a circle to have angular momentum.

topics.title: Collisions with Rotation
topics.short: When a ball sticks to a pivoted rod, angular momentum about the pivot is conserved but linear momentum is not.
topics.trouble: Students conserve linear momentum even though the pivot pushes on the rod.

topics.title: Work and Power in Rotation
topics.short: W = ∫τ dθ and P = τω.
topics.trouble: Students multiply the torque by an angle in degrees, or by the arc length.

topics.title: Gyroscopes and Precession
topics.short: A torque at right angles to the spin turns the direction of L, so a top precesses at Ω = τ/L.
topics.trouble: Students expect a spinning top to fall over rather than swing slowly around.

topics.title: Static Equilibrium Problems
topics.short: For ladders, hinged beams and hanging signs, choose a pivot that removes the unknowns you don't need.
topics.trouble: Students think a hinge's force on a beam must point along the beam.

topics.title: Gravity of a Spherical Body
topics.short: Outside a uniform sphere, gravity acts as if all the mass sat at the center; inside, g grows in proportion to r.
topics.trouble: Students think gravity is strongest at the center of the Earth.

topics.title: Orbital Energy
topics.short: A circular orbit has E = −GMm/(2r), so climbing to a higher orbit takes energy yet leaves you moving more slowly.
topics.trouble: Students think a satellite in a higher orbit must move faster.

topics.title: Kepler's Second Law from Angular Momentum
topics.short: Gravity exerts no torque about the Sun, so L is constant and equal areas are swept in equal times.
topics.trouble: Students think a planet moves at the same speed all around an elliptical orbit.

topics.title: Kepler's Third Law from Newton
topics.short: For a circular orbit T² = 4π²r³/(GM), which weighs a planet or star from its satellites.
topics.trouble: Students include the satellite's mass, which cancels, or use the altitude instead of the distance from the center.

topics.title: Speed on an Elliptical Orbit
topics.short: v² = GM(2/r − 1/a) gives the speed anywhere on an ellipse, which plans transfer orbits.
topics.trouble: Students think a rocket burn changes the height of the orbit right where the burn happens, rather than on the far side.

topics.title: The Equation of Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.short: x″ = −ω²x is solved by x = A cos(ωt + φ) with ω = √(k/m).
topics.trouble: Students mix up the angular frequency ω (rad/s) with the frequency f (Hz).

topics.title: Amplitude and Phase from Starting Conditions
topics.short: Use x(0) and v(0) to find the amplitude A and the phase φ.
topics.trouble: Students pick the phase without checking the sign of the starting velocity.

topics.title: Springs Hanging Vertically
topics.short: Gravity only moves the equilibrium point; the period stays 2π√(m/k).
topics.trouble: Students think gravity changes the period of a hanging spring.

topics.title: Simple and Physical Pendulums
topics.short: A swinging rigid body has T = 2π√(I/(mgd)), and small angles make any pendulum simple harmonic.
topics.trouble: Students use the whole length of a swinging rod instead of the distance from the pivot to its center of mass.

topics.title: Damped Oscillations
topics.short: Drag makes the amplitude shrink as e^(−bt/2m), and too much damping stops the swinging altogether.
topics.trouble: Students think a critically damped system swings once before it stops.

topics.title: Driven Oscillations and Resonance
topics.short: Pushing near the natural frequency builds a large amplitude, limited only by damping.
topics.trouble: Students think any repeated push makes the amplitude grow without limit.
